decks.title: Protista, Fungi, Lichens and Viruses — Part 1: Protists and the fungal body
goals: Give two characteristics and two examples of each protist group and compare locomotion in rhizopods, flagellates and ciliates
State the general characteristics of fungi and define plasmogamy, karyogamy and dikaryophase

slides.heading: Protists and fungi
slides.body_md: Part 1: single-celled eukaryotes, then the fungi and how their cells combine.

visual.alt: Flow from protists to fungi to sexual stages

slides.narration: This part looks at two kingdoms of eukaryotes. First the protists, mostly single-celled organisms that live in water. Then the fungi, with their threads called hyphae, and the stages by which fungal cells combine in sexual reproduction.

slides.heading: Kingdom Protista
slides.body_md: Protists are unicellular eukaryotes, mostly aquatic, and form a link between the prokaryotes and the other eukaryotic kingdoms.

rows: Diatoms and golden algae; silica shells that persist as diatomaceous earth; photosynthetic
Cell wall with cellulose plates; two flagella; some cause red tides
No cell wall but a flexible pellicle; two flagella; photosynthetic in light, feed on organisms in the dark
Saprophytes that form a creeping mass, the plasmodium, and spore-bearing fruiting bodies

visual.alt: Table of four protist groups with characteristics and examples

slides.narration: Chrysophytes have glassy shells of silica. Dinoflagellates have plates of cellulose and two flagella. Euglenoids have a flexible pellicle and can both photosynthesise and feed. Slime moulds creep over decaying matter and form spores.

slides.heading: Protozoans and how they move
slides.body_md: Protozoans are animal-like protists, grouped by their way of moving.

visual.alt: Table of four groups of protozoans with locomotion and examples

slides.narration: Rhizopods creep with pseudopodia, which are temporary false feet. Flagellates swim with one or more flagella. Ciliates are covered with cilia. Sporozoans, such as the malarial parasite, have no organ of movement and form infective spore-like stages.

slides.heading: Pseudopodia, flagella and cilia
slides.body_md: Compare the three kinds of locomotory organ.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a pond sample
slides.body_md: A drop of pond water holds 200 protozoans: 80 flagellates, 50 ciliates, 40 rhizopods and the rest of other kinds. Find the percentage of each group.
bullets: Flagellates = 80 ÷ 200 × 100 = **40 percent**; ciliates = **25 percent**.
Rhizopods = **20 percent**; others = **15 percent**.

visual.alt: Worked table of the percentage of each protozoan group in the sample

slides.narration: First find the number left over, thirty, by subtraction. Then divide each group by two hundred and multiply by one hundred. Flagellates make forty percent, ciliates twenty-five percent, rhizopods twenty percent and the others fifteen percent.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading the sample
slides.body_md: Use the same sample. What percentage of the protozoans are ciliates?
slides.narration: Quick check. Divide the number of ciliates by the total.

slides.heading: Kingdom Fungi
slides.body_md: Fungi are heterotrophic eukaryotes that absorb food; most are multicellular filaments.

rows: A network of threads called hyphae, forming a mycelium; yeast is unicellular
Saprophytic, parasitic or symbiotic; digestive enzymes are released and the food is absorbed
Vegetative (fragmentation, budding), asexual spores and sexual spores

visual.alt: Table of general characteristics of fungi

slides.narration: A fungus is a mass of hyphae. Its walls contain chitin. It releases enzymes onto dead matter or a living host and absorbs the digested food. It stores glycogen and oil and multiplies by fragments, buds and spores.

slides.heading: Kinds of hyphae
slides.body_md: Hyphae may be **aseptate and coenocytic** (no cross walls, many nuclei) or **septate** (with cross walls).

visual.alt: Coenocytic and septate fungal hyphae

slides.narration: In a coenocytic hypha the cytoplasm is one continuous tube with many nuclei. In a septate hypha, cross walls with small pores divide the thread into compartments, each with one or two nuclei.

slides.heading: Spores and kinds of sexual union
slides.body_md: Fungi make **asexual spores** (sporangiospores, conidia) and **sexual spores** (zygospores, ascospores, basidiospores). Sexual union is classified by the gametes.

rows: Fusion of two gametes alike in size and form
Fusion of two gametes of different size
Fusion of a small motile male gamete with a large non-motile female gamete

visual.alt: Table of isogamy, anisogamy and oogamy

slides.narration: If the two gametes look alike, the union is isogamy. If they differ in size, it is anisogamy. In oogamy a small motile male gamete fuses with a large stationary egg.

slides.heading: Plasmogamy, dikaryophase and karyogamy
slides.body_md: Fusion of fungal cells takes place in two steps, with a pause between them.

nodes.label: Hyphae of two mating types meet
Dikaryophase: two separate haploid nuclei in one cell

visual.alt: Flow of plasmogamy, dikaryophase and karyogamy

slides.narration: Plasmogamy is the fusion of cytoplasm of two cells. The nuclei do not fuse at once. The cell holds two separate nuclei in a stage called the dikaryophase. Karyogamy is the later fusion of the two nuclei into one.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: counting nuclei and chromosomes
slides.body_md: Each haploid nucleus of a fungus has 4 chromosomes. Follow the numbers through the stages.
bullets: After plasmogamy: **2** nuclei with 4 chromosomes each, so **8** chromosomes in the cell.
In the dikaryophase the count stays at **8** chromosomes in two nuclei.
After karyogamy: **1** nucleus holding **8** chromosomes (diploid).

visual.alt: Worked table of nuclei and chromosomes in the three stages

slides.narration: Plasmogamy brings two haploid nuclei into one cell, so there are eight chromosomes in two nuclei. They stay that way through the dikaryophase. Karyogamy then fuses them into one diploid nucleus with eight chromosomes.

slides.heading: Quick check: dikaryotic cell
slides.body_md: Each haploid nucleus has 7 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are present altogether in a dikaryotic cell?
slides.narration: Quick check. Count the nuclei and the chromosomes in each.

slides.narration: Quick check. Think of the name of each locomotory organ.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Protista: chrysophytes, dinoflagellates, euglenoids, slime moulds and protozoans.
Protozoans: rhizopods (pseudopodia), flagellates (flagella), ciliates (cilia), sporozoans (none).
Fungi: hyphae and mycelium, chitin wall, absorptive nutrition; hyphae aseptate or septate.
Gametes: isogamy, anisogamy, oogamy; plasmogamy, dikaryophase, karyogamy.

visual.alt: Summary table of protozoan locomotion

slides.narration: To recap: protists include four algal and mould groups and four protozoan groups sorted by their organs of movement. Fungi are absorptive, with chitin walls and hyphae. Their sexual union passes through plasmogamy, the dikaryophase and karyogamy.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Link each protozoan group with its **organ of locomotion** and an **example**.
Define **plasmogamy** (cytoplasm fuses), **karyogamy** (nuclei fuse) and **dikaryophase** (two nuclei in one cell).
Do not describe fungal life cycles; **definitions** are enough.
Name the **chitin** wall when listing fungal features.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Pair every protozoan group with its organ of movement. Define the three stages of fungal union precisely. Do not describe life cycles. And mention chitin when listing fungal features.

goals: Classify a fungus into its class from given characters and state the uses of fungi
Distinguish ectomycorrhiza from endomycorrhiza and explain the partnership in a lichen
Draw and label TMV and a bacteriophage and distinguish viruses, viroids and prions

slides.heading: Classes, partnerships and viruses
slides.body_md: Part 2: the four fungal classes, living partnerships, and agents that are not cells.

visual.alt: Flow from fungal classes to partnerships to viruses

slides.narration: This part covers the four classes of fungi, two partnerships in which fungi live with other organisms, and finally viruses, viroids and prions, which are infectious agents that are not true cells.

slides.heading: Four classes of fungi
slides.body_md: Fungi are placed in classes by their hyphae and sexual spores.

visual.alt: Table of the four classes of fungi

slides.narration: Zygomycetes have aseptate hyphae and form zygospores. Ascomycetes make ascospores inside sacs called asci. Basidiomycetes make basidiospores on a club-shaped basidium. Deuteromycetes are those in which no sexual stage is known.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: which class?
slides.body_md: Place three moulds in their classes from the characters seen under the microscope.
bullets: Mould P: aseptate hyphae, zygospores: **Zygomycetes**.
Mould Q: septate hyphae, spores in sac-like asci: **Ascomycetes**.
Mould R: septate hyphae, only conidia, no sexual stage known: **Deuteromycetes**.

rows: Septate hyphae; no sexual stage known

visual.alt: Worked table placing three moulds in classes

slides.narration: Look at the hyphae first. Aseptate hyphae with zygospores mean Zygomycetes. Septate hyphae with spores in asci mean Ascomycetes. If no sexual stage has ever been seen, the fungus goes into Deuteromycetes.

slides.heading: Quick check: ascospores
slides.body_md: A fruiting body has 150 asci, each with 8 ascospores. How many ascospores does it carry?
slides.narration: Quick check. Multiply the number of asci by the spores in each.

slides.heading: Fungi in medicine, bakery and decomposition
slides.body_md: Fungi are useful in several ways.

rows: Ferments sugar to carbon dioxide, which makes dough rise
Break down dead matter and return minerals to the soil

visual.alt: Table of uses of fungi

slides.narration: Penicillium gives penicillin. Yeast ferments sugar, and the carbon dioxide it releases makes dough rise. Saprophytic fungi decompose dead matter and return minerals to the soil.

slides.body_md: A lichen is a **symbiosis** of a fungus (**mycobiont**) and an alga or cyanobacterium (**phycobiont**).

sections.heading: 1. Kingdom Protista
sections.body_md:
Protista are **unicellular eukaryotes**, mostly aquatic. They form a link between prokaryotes and the other eukaryotic kingdoms.
- **Chrysophytes:** diatoms and golden algae; the cell wall is in two overlapping halves impregnated with **silica**, which survives as **diatomaceous earth**; photosynthetic (examples: diatoms, desmids).
- **Dinoflagellates:** cell wall of stiff **cellulose plates**, **two flagella** (one in a groove, one trailing); some (*Gonyaulax*) multiply rapidly and cause **red tides**.
- **Euglenoids:** no wall but a flexible protein-rich **pellicle**; **two flagella**; **photosynthetic in light and heterotrophic in the dark** (*Euglena*).
- **Slime moulds:** saprophytes that move over decaying matter forming a mass of cytoplasm, the **plasmodium**, which produces spore-bearing fruiting bodies (*Physarum*).
- **Protozoans** (heterotrophic, predators or parasites): **rhizopods** or amoeboid protozoans move by **pseudopodia** (*Amoeba*, *Entamoeba*); **flagellates** by **flagella** (*Trypanosoma*, *Giardia*); **ciliates** by **cilia** (*Paramecium*); **sporozoans** have **no locomotory organ** and an infective spore-like stage (*Plasmodium*).

sections.heading: 2. Kingdom Fungi: general characteristics, spores and sexual reproduction
sections.body_md:
Fungi are **heterotrophic eukaryotes** that absorb their food (saprophytes, parasites or symbionts). The body is a network of **hyphae** forming a **mycelium** (yeast is unicellular). Walls are of **chitin**; food is stored as **glycogen and oil**. Hyphae are **aseptate and coenocytic** (no cross walls, many nuclei) or **septate** (cross walls with pores).

Reproduction is vegetative (fragmentation, budding), **asexual** (sporangiospores, conidia) and **sexual** (zygospores, ascospores, basidiospores). Sexual union can be classified by the gametes: **isogamy** (gametes alike), **anisogamy** (gametes unequal in size) and **oogamy** (small motile male gamete and large non-motile egg).

Fusion occurs in stages: **plasmogamy** is the fusion of the cytoplasm of two cells; the nuclei stay separate in the **dikaryophase** (two haploid nuclei in one cell); **karyogamy** is the fusion of the two nuclei to form a diploid nucleus. With a haploid number of 4, the dikaryotic cell holds 8 chromosomes in two nuclei and the nucleus after karyogamy holds 8. **Life cycles of fungi are not required**; only these terms are.

key_terms.definition_md: The network of hyphae that forms the body of a fungus.
Fusion of the cytoplasm of two cells.
The stage in which a cell contains two separate haploid nuclei.
Fusion of the two haploid nuclei to form a diploid nucleus.
Fusion of similar gametes, of unequal gametes, and of a small motile male with a large non-motile female gamete.

sections.heading: 3. Classes of fungi, uses, lichens and mycorrhiza
sections.body_md:
| Class | Hyphae | Sexual spore | Asexual spore | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Zygomycetes | Aseptate, coenocytic | Zygospore | Sporangiospores | Mucor, Rhizopus |
| Ascomycetes | Septate | Ascospores in asci | Conidia | Penicillium, Aspergillus, Neurospora, yeast |
| Basidiomycetes | Septate | Basidiospores on a basidium | Usually absent | Agaricus, Ustilago, Puccinia |
| Deuteromycetes | Septate | Not known | Conidia | Alternaria, Colletotrichum, Trichoderma |

**Uses:** *Penicillium* gives the antibiotic **penicillin** (medicine); **yeast** ferments sugar to carbon dioxide and alcohol, so dough rises and bread is baked (bakery); saprophytic fungi **decompose** dead matter and return minerals to the soil.

**Lichens** are symbiotic associations of a fungus (**mycobiont**) and an alga or cyanobacterium (**phycobiont**): the alga photosynthesises and the fungus gives shelter, water and minerals. They are very slow-growing and sensitive to sulphur dioxide, so they are **pollution indicators**.

**Mycorrhiza** is an association between a fungus and plant roots: the fungus absorbs water and minerals (especially phosphorus) and the plant supplies sugars. In **ectomycorrhiza** (pine) the fungus forms a **sheath outside the root** and its hyphae lie between the cortical cells; in **endomycorrhiza** the hyphae **penetrate into the cortical cells** (vesicular-arbuscular mycorrhiza).

A symbiotic association of a fungus with the roots of a plant.
A mycorrhiza in which the fungus forms a sheath around the root and its hyphae stay between cortical cells.
A mycorrhiza in which the fungal hyphae enter the cortical cells of the root.

sections.heading: 4. Viruses, viroids and prions
sections.body_md:
**Viruses** link the living and the non-living: outside a host they are inert and can be crystallised, yet inside a host cell they multiply and mutate. A virus is a **nucleic acid** (DNA or RNA) in a **protein coat (capsid)** made of **capsomeres**.

**Discovery:** **D. J. Ivanowsky** (1892) found that sap of diseased tobacco plants still infected healthy plants after passing through a filter that stops bacteria. **M. W. Beijerinck** (1898) called the agent **contagium vivum fluidum** (infectious living fluid). **W. M. Stanley** (1935) crystallised the virus and showed that it is mainly protein with RNA.

**Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV):** a straight helical rod about 300 nanometres long and 18 nanometres wide, with a helical capsid of capsomeres around a single strand of **RNA**. **Bacteriophage:** a **hexagonal head** with **double-stranded DNA**, a **collar**, a **tail** with a **contractile sheath**, a **base plate** and **tail fibres**.

**Viroids** (T. O. Diener, 1971): infectious **free RNA** of low molecular weight, with no protein coat (potato spindle tuber disease). **Prions:** infectious **abnormally folded proteins** with no nucleic acid, causing **BSE** (bovine spongiform encephalopathy) in cattle and **CJD** (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease) in humans.

key_terms.definition_md: The protein coat of a virus, made of capsomeres.
An infectious agent made only of a short free RNA molecule.
An infectious agent made only of an abnormally folded protein.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving the wrong organ of locomotion for a protozoan group (sporozoans have none).
- Describing fungal life cycles; the syllabus asks only for the terms plasmogamy, karyogamy and dikaryophase.
- Confusing plasmogamy (cytoplasm fuses) with karyogamy (nuclei fuse).
- Placing a fungus in a class without using the hyphae and the sexual spore.
- Saying that mycorrhiza harms the plant; it is a partnership in which both gain.
- Writing that a prion contains DNA or RNA; it is protein only.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a term, an example, a scientist, a year, a count, an analogy or a give-a-reason.
- 2–3-mark questions: protist groups with locomotion; stages of fungal union; classes of fungi; ecto- against endomycorrhiza; viruses against viroids and prions.
- 5-mark questions in parts: protozoans and protists compared; fungal classes with uses; lichens and mycorrhiza; TMV and bacteriophage with labelled diagrams and the history of viruses.

Head with DNA, collar, tail sheath, base plate, tail fibres.

questions.stem_md: Thick layers of glassy powder dug from an old lake bed are the remains of microscopic algae that lived there. Which substance made the walls of these algae so durable?
questions.solution_md: The walls of diatoms are impregnated with silica, which does not decay — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which pair of features is correct for dinoflagellates?

options.text_md: A silica shell in two halves and no flagella
A flexible pellicle and a single flagellum
Stiff cellulose plates in the wall and two flagella

questions.solution_md: Dinoflagellates have cellulose plates and two flagella — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A culture of Euglena is kept in complete darkness for several weeks in water rich in dissolved food and tiny organisms. It stays alive because it can
questions.solution_md: Without light Euglena behaves as a heterotroph, feeding on small organisms — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A multinucleate mass of cytoplasm creeps slowly over rotting logs, feeding on dead matter, and later forms stalked structures that release spores. This creeping mass is called a
questions.solution_md: The feeding body of a slime mould is the plasmodium — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A slide of pond water shows a slipper-shaped cell that glides smoothly by the coordinated beating of many short projections over its surface. It is a
questions.solution_md: Many short beating projections are cilia, so the cell is a ciliate — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which group of protozoans has no organ of locomotion?
questions.solution_md: Sporozoans, such as the malarial parasite, have no locomotory organ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Entamoeba, a parasite of the human intestine, belongs to the rhizopods. How does it move?

options.text_md: It does not move at all

questions.solution_md: Rhizopods move by pseudopodia — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A pond sample holds 200 protozoans: 80 flagellates, 50 ciliates, 40 rhizopods and the rest of other kinds. What percentage are of other kinds?
In a pond sample of 200 protozoans, 80 are flagellates, 50 are ciliates and 40 are rhizopods. What percentage of the protozoans are ciliates?
Match each protozoan group in column I with its way of moving in column II.
questions.solution_md: Rhizopods use pseudopodia, flagellates flagella, ciliates cilia, and sporozoans have no locomotory organ.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.

questions.stem_md: Compare the locomotion of rhizopods and ciliates, giving one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Rhizopods** such as *Amoeba* move by **pseudopodia**, temporary extensions of the cell that flow forward. **Ciliates** such as *Paramecium* move by the coordinated beating of numerous short **cilia** covering the body.

questions.solution_md: Pseudopodia; cilia.

questions.stem_md: Give two characteristics and two examples of chrysophytes.

answer.model_answer_md: Chrysophytes are **photosynthetic** and have cell walls in two overlapping halves **impregnated with silica**, which remain as **diatomaceous earth**. Examples are **diatoms** and **desmids**.

questions.solution_md: Two characteristics; two examples.

questions.stem_md: Describe the body of a slime mould and say how it obtains its food.

answer.model_answer_md: The body is a creeping, multinucleate mass of cytoplasm called a **plasmodium**. It moves over decaying logs and leaves and feeds as a **saprophyte** on dead organic matter; under unfavourable conditions it forms spore-bearing fruiting bodies.

questions.solution_md: Plasmodium; saprophytic.

questions.stem_md: Give one characteristic and one example of each of three groups of protozoans.

answer.model_answer_md: **Rhizopods** move by **pseudopodia** (*Amoeba*). **Flagellates** move by **flagella** and include parasites (*Trypanosoma*). **Ciliates** are covered with **cilia** (*Paramecium*). **Sporozoans** have **no locomotory organ** and an infective spore-like stage (*Plasmodium*).

questions.solution_md: Three groups with a feature and an example.

questions.stem_md: Compare dinoflagellates and euglenoids with respect to the cell covering, the flagella and the mode of nutrition.

answer.model_answer_md: **Dinoflagellates** have a wall of stiff **cellulose plates**, **two flagella** and are mostly photosynthetic. **Euglenoids** have no wall but a flexible protein-rich **pellicle**, **two flagella**, and are **photosynthetic in light** and **heterotrophic in the dark**.

questions.solution_md: Cell covering; flagella; nutrition.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name the four groups of protozoans and state how each moves. [2]
(b) State two features of euglenoids. [2]
(c) Name the group of protists that cause red tides. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Rhizopods** (pseudopodia), **flagellates** (flagella), **ciliates** (cilia) and **sporozoans** (no locomotory organ).

(b) Euglenoids have **no cell wall but a flexible pellicle**, **two flagella**, and are **photosynthetic in light and heterotrophic in the dark**.

(c) The **dinoflagellates**.

questions.solution_md: Four groups; two features; dinoflagellates.

questions.stem_md: Which pair of features is true of the body of a typical fungus?

options.text_md: A single cell with walls of silica
Tissues and organs with walls of peptidoglycan

questions.solution_md: Fungi are made of hyphae with chitin in the walls — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Under the microscope a fungal thread is seen as one continuous tube with many nuclei scattered in its cytoplasm and no cross walls. The hypha is

options.text_md: septate with one nucleus per cell
septate with a pore in each wall

questions.solution_md: No cross walls and many nuclei describe an aseptate, coenocytic hypha — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In a fungus, two gametes of different sizes fuse. This kind of sexual union is
questions.solution_md: Fusion of gametes of unequal size is anisogamy — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Two fungal hyphae of different mating types meet and their cytoplasm fuses, but the nuclei stay separate. This event is
questions.solution_md: Fusion of the cytoplasm of two cells is plasmogamy — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A fungal cell is found to contain two genetically different haploid nuclei lying side by side. This stage is
questions.solution_md: Two separate haploid nuclei in one cell define the dikaryophase — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Each haploid nucleus of a fungus has 7 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are present altogether in a dikaryotic cell?
questions.solution_md: A dikaryotic cell has 2 nuclei of 7 chromosomes each: 2 × 7 = 14.

questions.stem_md: The haploid nuclei of two mating hyphae each have 6 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in the single nucleus formed after karyogamy?
questions.solution_md: The two nuclei fuse: 6 + 6 = 12 chromosomes (diploid).

questions.stem_md: A flask is seeded with 5 yeast cells. If the cells double every 90 minutes, how many cells are present after 6 hours?
questions.solution_md: 360 / 90 = 4 generations: 5 × 2 to the power 4 = 5 × 16 = 80.

questions.stem_md: The fusion of the two haploid nuclei in the sexual reproduction of a fungus is called ______.
questions.solution_md: Karyogamy.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Aseptate hyphae are divided into compartments by cross walls.
questions.solution_md: False. Septate hyphae have cross walls; aseptate hyphae have none and are coenocytic.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In many fungi, karyogamy follows plasmogamy only after a delay.

**Reason (R):** Plasmogamy is the fusion of the cytoplasm of two cells.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the meaning of plasmogamy does not explain why the nuclei fuse later — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: Fungi are not placed in the plant kingdom.

answer.model_answer_md: Fungi are **heterotrophic** and **absorb** their food, and their walls are made of **chitin** and not cellulose.

questions.solution_md: Heterotrophic; chitin.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between isogamy, anisogamy and oogamy in one line each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Isogamy:** fusion of two gametes alike in size and form. **Anisogamy:** fusion of two gametes of different size. **Oogamy:** fusion of a small motile male gamete with a large non-motile female gamete.

questions.solution_md: Three one-line definitions.

questions.stem_md: Define the dikaryophase and state at what point in sexual reproduction it begins.

answer.model_answer_md: The **dikaryophase** is the stage in which a cell contains **two separate haploid nuclei**. It begins after **plasmogamy**, when the cytoplasm of two cells has fused, and ends when the nuclei fuse in **karyogamy**.

questions.solution_md: Two nuclei in one cell; after plasmogamy.

questions.stem_md: State three general characteristics of fungi and name the material of their cell wall.

answer.model_answer_md: Fungi are **heterotrophic**, absorbing food after digesting it with enzymes released outside the body. The body is made of threads called **hyphae** forming a **mycelium**, and food is stored as **glycogen and oil**. The cell wall is made of **chitin**.

questions.solution_md: Three characteristics; chitin.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name the two kinds of fungal hyphae and state how they differ. [2]
(b) Define plasmogamy, dikaryophase and karyogamy. [2]
(c) Name the four classes of fungi. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Aseptate (coenocytic)** hyphae have **no cross walls** and many nuclei in continuous cytoplasm; **septate** hyphae are divided by **cross walls** with pores into compartments.

(b) **Plasmogamy:** fusion of the cytoplasm of two cells. **Dikaryophase:** a stage with **two separate haploid nuclei** in one cell. **Karyogamy:** fusion of the two nuclei into one diploid nucleus.

(c) **Zygomycetes, Ascomycetes, Basidiomycetes and Deuteromycetes.**

questions.solution_md: Two hyphae types; three definitions; four classes.

questions.stem_md: Which pair correctly matches a fungus with its class?
questions.solution_md: Puccinia bears basidiospores and is a basidiomycete. Mucor is a zygomycete, Trichoderma a deuteromycete and Neurospora an ascomycete — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A mould has septate hyphae and produces its sexual spores in tiny sac-like structures called asci. To which class does it belong?
questions.solution_md: Spores formed inside asci mark the Ascomycetes — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A soil fungus forms only conidia. After years of study no sexual stage has been seen. Which class is it placed in?
questions.solution_md: A fungus whose sexual stage is not known goes into Deuteromycetes — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which fungus is the source of the antibiotic penicillin?
questions.solution_md: Penicillin is obtained from species of Penicillium — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In a lichen, which statement correctly divides the work between the partners?

options.text_md: The fungus makes food by photosynthesis and the alga absorbs minerals
Both partners make food by photosynthesis
The alga makes food by photosynthesis and the fungus supplies shelter, water and minerals

questions.solution_md: The phycobiont photosynthesises and the mycobiont gives shelter, water and minerals — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Lichens that once covered the walls of a town slowly disappear after a coal-burning power station is built nearby. Which pollutant is the most likely cause?
questions.solution_md: Lichens are very sensitive to sulphur dioxide — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A fungal sheath covers the root tips of a pine seedling. Its hyphae lie between the cortical cells but do not enter them. This association is
questions.solution_md: A sheath outside the root with hyphae between the cells is ectomycorrhiza — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A fruiting body of an ascomycete has 150 asci, and each ascus holds 8 ascospores. How many ascospores does it carry?

questions.solution_md: Mycobiont.

questions.stem_md:

**Reason (R):** Lichens are very sensitive to sulphur dioxide in the air.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: lichens fail to grow where the air has sulphur dioxide — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Name the fungus used in (i) the making of an antibiotic and (ii) baking, and state the product in each case.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) ***Penicillium*** produces the antibiotic **penicillin**. (ii) **Yeast** (*Saccharomyces*) ferments sugar and releases **carbon dioxide**, which makes the dough rise.

questions.solution_md: Penicillium; yeast.

marking_scheme.step: Yeast and carbon dioxide in dough

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between ectomycorrhiza and endomycorrhiza on the position of the fungal hyphae.

answer.model_answer_md: In **ectomycorrhiza** the fungus forms a **sheath around the root** and its hyphae lie **between** the cortical cells. In **endomycorrhiza** the hyphae **penetrate into** the cortical cells of the root.

questions.solution_md: Sheath outside; hyphae inside cells.

questions.stem_md: Explain why lichens are rare in a heavily polluted town.

answer.model_answer_md: Lichens are **very sensitive to air pollutants**, especially **sulphur dioxide**, which damages the algal partner and stops growth. Their absence therefore shows polluted air, and their presence shows clean air.

questions.solution_md: Sensitive to sulphur dioxide.

questions.stem_md: Name the class of each of these fungi and the sexual spore it forms: (i) Rhizopus, (ii) Aspergillus, (iii) Ustilago.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) *Rhizopus* is a **Zygomycete** and forms **zygospores**. (ii) *Aspergillus* is an **Ascomycete** and forms **ascospores** in asci. (iii) *Ustilago* is a **Basidiomycete** and forms **basidiospores** on a basidium. Characters: Zygomycetes, Ascomycetes and Basidiomycetes.

questions.solution_md: Three classes and spores.

questions.stem_md: Explain the partnership in a lichen. State what each partner supplies and give the scientific terms for the two partners.

answer.model_answer_md: A lichen is a **symbiosis** of a fungus, the **mycobiont**, and an alga or cyanobacterium, the **phycobiont**. The **alga photosynthesises** and supplies food; the **fungus** gives **shelter, water and minerals** and protects the alga. Both partners gain.

questions.solution_md: Symbiosis; two terms; contributions.

marking_scheme.step: Fungus supplies shelter, water and minerals

questions.stem_md: Describe the partnership called mycorrhiza and say how each partner benefits.

answer.model_answer_md: A **mycorrhiza** is an association between a **fungus and the roots** of a plant. The fungus absorbs **water and minerals**, especially phosphorus, from the soil and passes them to the plant; the plant supplies **sugars** to the fungus. Both partners gain, so it is a **symbiosis**.

questions.solution_md: Association; fungus gives minerals; plant gives sugars.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name the two partners of a lichen and state what each contributes. [2]
(b) Distinguish ectomycorrhiza from endomycorrhiza. [2]
(c) Why are lichens used as pollution indicators? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The **mycobiont (fungus)** gives shelter, water and minerals; the **phycobiont (alga or cyanobacterium)** makes food by photosynthesis.

(b) In **ectomycorrhiza** the fungus forms a **sheath outside the root** and its hyphae lie between cortical cells; in **endomycorrhiza** the **hyphae enter** the cortical cells.

(c) Lichens are **very sensitive to air pollution**, especially **sulphur dioxide**, so they disappear from polluted places.

questions.solution_md: Partners; two types of mycorrhiza; indicator.

They make their own food but cannot move

questions.solution_md: Viruses are inert and crystallisable outside a host, yet multiply and mutate inside one — option (b).

questions.stem_md: What is the main structural difference between a viroid and a virus?

options.text_md: A viroid has a double protein coat
A viroid is larger than a virus
A viroid has no protein coat

questions.solution_md: A viroid is a short free RNA with no protein coat — option (d).

questions.stem_md: An infectious agent is isolated from the brain of a diseased animal. It survives treatments that destroy nucleic acids but is destroyed by protein-digesting enzymes. It is most likely a
questions.solution_md: An infectious agent made only of protein is a prion — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which scientist described the infectious fluid of tobacco mosaic disease as a contagium vivum fluidum?
questions.solution_md: Beijerinck used this phrase in 1898 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Ivanowsky made his observation on tobacco mosaic disease in 1892, and Diener discovered viroids in 1971. How many years separate the two discoveries?
Beijerinck named the infectious fluid in 1898, and Stanley crystallised a virus in 1935. How many years passed between these two events?
True or false? A prion consists of DNA enclosed in a protein coat.
questions.solution_md: False. A prion is an abnormally folded protein with no nucleic acid.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Viruses can multiply in a sterile nutrient broth without any living cells.

**Reason (R):** Viruses possess their own ribosomes for making proteins.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are false: viruses multiply only inside a host cell and have no ribosomes of their own — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Prions cause bovine spongiform encephalopathy in cattle.

**Reason (R):** Prions contain RNA enclosed in a protein coat.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: a prion is protein only — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Complete the analogy: Bacteriophage : double-stranded DNA :: Tobacco mosaic virus : ______

answer.model_answer_md: **Single-stranded RNA**.

questions.solution_md: RNA.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: Viruses are called obligate parasites.

answer.model_answer_md: Viruses have **no metabolic machinery of their own** and can multiply **only inside a living host cell**.

questions.solution_md: Multiply only in host cells.

marking_scheme.step: Can multiply only inside a host cell

questions.stem_md: State two reasons for regarding viruses as a link between the living and the non-living.

answer.model_answer_md: Outside a host a virus is **inert and can be crystallised**, like a non-living chemical. Inside a living cell it **multiplies and mutates**, using the host machinery, like a living organism.

questions.solution_md: Crystallised outside; multiply inside.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish a viroid from a prion on the basis of composition, and name a disease of cattle caused by one of them.

answer.model_answer_md: A **viroid** is a short piece of **free RNA** with no protein coat. A **prion** is an **abnormally folded protein** with no nucleic acid. Prions cause **bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE)** in cattle.

questions.solution_md: RNA only; protein only; BSE.

questions.stem_md: Describe the structure of tobacco mosaic virus, naming its coat, the units that build the coat and its genetic material.

answer.model_answer_md: Tobacco mosaic virus is a **helical rod**. Its protein coat, the **capsid**, is built of many identical subunits called **capsomeres** wound in a helix. Inside it runs a **single strand of RNA**, the genetic material.

questions.solution_md: Rod; capsid and capsomeres; RNA.

questions.stem_md: Name five parts of a bacteriophage and state the function of any two of them.

answer.model_answer_md: The parts are the **head** with double-stranded DNA, the **collar**, the **tail sheath and core**, the **base plate** and the **tail fibres**. The **tail fibres** attach the phage to a bacterium, and the **contractile sheath** pushes the core through the bacterial wall so that the DNA is injected.

questions.solution_md: Five parts; two functions.

questions.stem_md: State the contribution of Ivanowsky, of Beijerinck and of Stanley to the study of viruses.

answer.model_answer_md: **Ivanowsky** (1892) showed that sap of diseased tobacco still infected healthy plants after passing a bacteria-stopping filter. **Beijerinck** (1898) called the agent a **contagium vivum fluidum**. **Stanley** (1935) **crystallised** the virus and showed it to be mainly protein and RNA.

questions.solution_md: Three contributions.

questions.stem_md: Compare a virus, a viroid and a prion in terms of what each contains. Give one example of a disease or host for each.

answer.model_answer_md: A **virus** has **nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) in a protein coat**, as in tobacco mosaic virus or a bacteriophage. A **viroid** is **free RNA with no coat**, as in potato spindle tuber disease. A **prion** is an **abnormally folded protein** with no nucleic acid, as in BSE of cattle.

questions.solution_md: Three agents compared.

questions.stem_md: A diseased sheep’s brain yields an infectious extract. Treatment with an enzyme that destroys DNA and RNA does not reduce infectivity, but an enzyme that digests protein does. What kind of agent is it? Explain why it is neither a virus nor a viroid.

answer.model_answer_md: It is a **prion**. Its infectivity survives **nucleic-acid-digesting enzymes** but not **protein-digesting enzymes**, so it is made of **protein only**. A **virus** contains DNA or RNA in a protein coat and a **viroid** is free RNA; since this agent has **no nucleic acid**, it can be neither.

questions.solution_md: Prion; no nucleic acid.

marking_scheme.step: Why not a virus or a viroid

(a) Draw a labelled diagram of tobacco mosaic virus. [2]
(b) Name five parts of a bacteriophage. [2]
(c) State the contribution of W. M. Stanley to the study of viruses. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:

(b) **Head, collar, tail sheath, base plate and tail fibres** (the head contains double-stranded DNA).

(c) **Stanley** crystallised the virus in 1935 and showed that it is mainly protein with RNA.

questions.solution_md: TMV diagram; five phage parts; Stanley.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
A student counts the protozoans in a drop of hay-infusion culture.

| Type of cell | Number |
|---|---|
| Amoeba-like cells | 18 |
| Flagellated cells | 30 |
| Ciliated cells | 24 |
| Other kinds | 8 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 30 %

**(b)** (c) By pseudopodia

**(c)** (i) The ciliated cells move by **cilia**, short hair-like structures that beat together. A common example is ***Paramecium***.

**OR** (ii) The flagellated cells move by **flagella**, long whip-like structures. A parasitic example is ***Trypanosoma***.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Total = 80; 24 / 80 × 100 = 30 percent.

**(b)** Amoeboid cells are rhizopods and move by pseudopodia — option (c).

**(c)** (i) Cilia; Paramecium.

(ii) Flagella; Trypanosoma.

children.stem_md: What percentage of the protozoans counted are ciliated?
How do the amoeba-like cells move?

options.text_md: They have no way of moving

children.solution_md: Amoeboid cells are rhizopods and move by pseudopodia — option (c).

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Name the organ of locomotion of the ciliated cells and the genus of a common example.

answer.model_answer_md: The ciliated cells move by **cilia**, short hair-like structures that beat together. A common example is ***Paramecium***.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Name the organ of locomotion of the flagellated cells and give one parasitic example of this group.

answer.model_answer_md: The flagellated cells move by **flagella**, long whip-like structures. A parasitic example is ***Trypanosoma***.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
A laboratory studies three infectious agents.

| Agent | Findings |
|---|---|
| W | DNA enclosed in a protein coat; infects bacteria |
| X | Protein only; no nucleic acid; found in diseased brain tissue |
| Y | Short free RNA with no protein coat; found in diseased coconut palms |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (b) X

**(b)** (a) A bacteriophage

**(c)** (i) Agent Y is a **viroid**. It consists only of **free RNA with no protein coat**, whereas a virus has nucleic acid enclosed in a protein coat.

**OR** (ii) Agent X contains **no nucleic acid**; it is an **abnormally folded protein**, so a treatment that destroys DNA and RNA has **no target** in it.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Protein only with no nucleic acid defines a prion — option (b).

**(b)** A virus that infects bacteria is a bacteriophage — option (a).

**(c)** (i) Viroid; no coat.

(ii) No nucleic acid; protein only.

children.solution_md: Protein only with no nucleic acid defines a prion — option (b).

children.stem_md: What is agent W most likely to be?
children.solution_md: A virus that infects bacteria is a bacteriophage — option (a).

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): What is agent Y, and why is it not a virus?

answer.model_answer_md: Agent Y is a **viroid**. It consists only of **free RNA with no protein coat**, whereas a virus has nucleic acid enclosed in a protein coat.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Why does a treatment that destroys all nucleic acids fail to make agent X harmless?

answer.model_answer_md: Agent X contains **no nucleic acid**; it is an **abnormally folded protein**, so a treatment that destroys DNA and RNA has **no target** in it.

questions.stem_md: A baker finds that dough made with old, dead yeast does not rise. Which product of living yeast is missing from the dough?

options.text_md: Carbon dioxide from fermentation of sugar

questions.solution_md: Living yeast ferments sugar and releases carbon dioxide, which makes the dough rise — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A bacteriophage attaches to a bacterium by its tail fibres and its sheath contracts. What enters the bacterial cell?

options.text_md: The whole phage including its tail
The DNA of the phage, while most of the coat stays outside

questions.solution_md: The phage injects its DNA and leaves the empty coat outside — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A pond cell has two flagella, no cell wall, a flexible protein-rich covering and green chloroplasts. It is most likely a
questions.solution_md: A pellicle in place of a wall with two flagella and chloroplasts marks a euglenoid — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Pine seedlings planted in sterilised soil, free of the fungi normally found around pine roots, grow poorly even though the soil has minerals. The best explanation is that

options.text_md: the fungus normally makes food for the seedling by photosynthesis
the seedling needs the fungus to fix atmospheric nitrogen in nodules
the mycorrhizal fungus that helps the roots absorb minerals is missing
fungi always harm the roots of pines

questions.solution_md: The mycorrhizal fungus normally helps absorption of water and minerals; without it growth is poor — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A tobacco mosaic virus particle is 300 nanometres long. How many such particles placed end to end would span 3 micrometres?
questions.solution_md: 3 micrometres = 3000 nanometres; 3000 / 300 = 10 particles.

questions.stem_md: A small mushroom cap bears 60 basidia, and each basidium carries its usual number of basidiospores. How many basidiospores does the cap carry?
questions.solution_md: A basidium bears 4 basidiospores: 60 × 4 = 240.

questions.stem_md: Under the microscope, fungal hyphae are seen entering the cortical cells of the root of a herb and branching inside them. This association is
questions.solution_md: Hyphae that penetrate the cortical cells make an endomycorrhiza — option (b).
